---
title: "The Regression Framework"
subtitle: "Where ordinary least squares sits, and what each method on this site changes about it"
---

## A model has five moving parts

### The five parts

Fitting a regression model means making five separate choices, whether or not they're stated explicitly:

1. **Estimand** — what aspect of $Y \mid X$ is actually being modeled. Ordinary least squares targets the conditional mean, $E[Y \mid X]$. A model could instead target the median or a quantile; that choice determines everything downstream.
2. **Random component** — how $Y$ scatters around that estimand. OLS assumes $Y_i \mid X_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma^2)$: Gaussian noise, the same variance at every value of $X$.
3. **Link function** — the function connecting the mean to the linear predictor, $g(\mu_i) = \eta_i$. OLS uses the **identity link**, $g(\mu) = \mu$, which is precisely why OLS doesn't feel like it has a link function at all — it has one, it just does nothing.
4. **Systematic component** — how the regressors combine into the linear predictor, $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \beta_2 X_{2i} + \cdots$.
5. **Estimation** — the numerical values of the $\beta$'s that fit the data. OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals; under the Gaussian assumption in step 2, that's identical to maximum likelihood.

### OLS as one specific setting

Ordinary least squares is one specific setting of all five: conditional mean, Gaussian noise, identity link, a linear-in-the-parameters systematic component, least squares. Every other method on this site changes one of those five slots and keeps the rest:

- A **generalized linear model** changes the link and/or the random component — a log link, Poisson or Gamma noise — while keeping the systematic component linear in $\beta$.
- A **generalized additive model** ([`gam.qmd`](gam.qmd)) changes the systematic component, from $\beta_0 + \beta_1 X$ to $\beta_0 + f(X)$, a smooth function estimated from the data instead of a single coefficient times $X$ — while keeping the identity link and Gaussian random component.
- A **generalized additive mixed model** ([`gamm.qmd`](gamm.qmd)) changes neither the mean, the link, nor the systematic component — it changes what "random component" is allowed to mean, letting residuals be correlated with each other instead of requiring independence.

### What later chapters change

Framed this way, none of the methods on this site is a wholesale departure from OLS. Each one relaxes exactly one of the five assumptions above, in a specific, nameable way, while leaving the rest of the framework intact.

## "Linear" means linear in the coefficients, not straight in $X$

A regression is a **linear model** if the systematic component is a linear combination of terms — linear in the $\beta$'s — regardless of whether those terms are linear functions of the original regressor. `lm(y ~ x + I(x^2))` fits

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 x_i^2 + \varepsilon_i,$$

which produces a curved fitted line in $x$ while remaining a linear model: the fit is still a linear combination of the columns $\{1, x, x^2\}$, estimated the same way a simple straight line would be. [`piecewise-regression.qmd`](piecewise-regression.qmd) uses the same trick with a hinge term instead of a squared term — $\beta_2 (x_i - c)_+$, where $(x - c)_+ = \max(0, x - c)$ — one more column handed to `lm()`, not a different kind of model. Feature-engineering the regressor bends the fitted curve without ever leaving step 4 of the framework above; it's a different move from transforming the response or changing the link (see [Transformations](transformations.qmd)).

## Multiple regressors, and why visualizability breaks down the way it does

A single continuous regressor gives a fit that's a line or curve in two dimensions — fully visualizable. Two continuous regressors give a fit that's a surface in three dimensions — still visualizable, if harder to draw by hand. Three or more continuous regressors give a fit with no direct picture at all; it's still "linear in the $\beta$'s," it just can't be drawn.

A **categorical** regressor doesn't add a dimension the same way a second continuous regressor does. It doesn't turn a 2D fit into a 3D one — it produces a family of lines within the same 2D picture, one per category, either parallel (an additive model) or free to diverge (an interaction model). This project only ever has one regressor — time — so that distinction is never exercised in the case studies here; it matters for reading models elsewhere, such as the year-by-monitoring-area trend models in the sibling `vignette-temporal-trends` project, where "area" is exactly this kind of categorical regressor.

## What comes next

The rest of this site works through methods that each change one slot of the framework above, in order of increasing flexibility: a hinge term on the regressor (piecewise regression), a mean shift at an unknown location (changepoint detection), fully nonparametric local averaging (k-nearest-neighbors, LOESS), a flexible smooth term with proper inference (GAM), and an explicit model for correlated residuals (GAMM). [Transformations](transformations.qmd), next, covers the response-side and regressor-side tools available before reaching for any of them — and how to tell which one a given series actually needs.
